findings.title: A rejected device can bypass the limit on its next request
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` caches the device ID before calling the store. When the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, this new return propagates the rejection but leaves that cache entry in place. On the next request from the same device, the cache hit skips the store call and returns success, so anonymous authentication is allowed despite the device limit. Only cache the ID after a successful store operation, or remove it when the operation fails.

findings.title: Concurrent registrations can exceed the configured device limit
findings.body: The count check and subsequent insert are separate, unprotected database operations. If the active count is one below the limit, concurrent requests for different device IDs can both observe room and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. Enforce the check and insert atomically or serialize competing registrations.

findings.title: A no-op MySQL update can be mistaken for a device-limit rejection
findings.body: This treats zero affected rows as proof that the device is absent. MySQL normally reports rows changed, not rows matched, so an update that leaves all stored values unchanged reports zero. In particular, `updated_at` can be stored at second precision, making a repeat update within the same second a no-op when IP and user agent are unchanged. At the limit, that valid existing device is then rejected. Distinguish absence from an unchanged update rather than relying on this affected-row check across database drivers.
